evidence: opened the landing page and read the hero, six feature blocks, the quote and the video section
opened /pricing at phone width and read the plan table, the footnote and the four questions
opened the sign-up page and read the form fields, the step indicator and the small print
opened the privacy page and read it
checked the stylesheet for how the pricing table behaves under 760 px
attempted the sign-up in my head: would type an email, stopped before the card number field
name: Hannah Brooks
first_10s: Okay, 'know what's in the fridge before you shop.' Fine. Cute phone mockup with a flat of roommates, Sam, Priya and Jo. That's not me, I have two kids and a husband. Oat milk, mustard times three, ha. I already have a shared list app with Dave on it and it's free. So what does this do that mine doesn't? Scan a receipt, expiry nudges. Hm. Show me the price.
journey: Landed on the home page. Hero is aimed at flatshares, the example pantry is 'Flat 3B' with roommates. Took a second to decide it could be for a family of four.
Scrolled the features. Expiry nudges and the waste report are the two things my current app does not do. 'Partner offers' based on my pantry made me pause.
Hit 'See how it works' and it jumps to a box that says the product tour video is coming soon. Nothing to watch.

Opened Pricing. On my phone the table is wider than the screen: I see the Starter column and half of Household. I had to swipe sideways to find out what I would actually pay. The price for Household is cut off at '$3.99/m'.
Swiped across and found $3.99/mo for Household (up to 5, fits us) but the asterisk says billed annually, $47.88 a year. Monthly is $5.99, hidden in the FAQ accordion.
Opened the card question: 'It keeps the trial smooth for your whole household.' That is not an answer.

Tapped 'Start 14-day trial'. Sign-up asks for email, a 12-character password and the card number on the very first screen, before I have seen the app do anything. It says I won't be charged today and the plan starts after the trial unless I cancel.
Stopped there. Would not type the card number. Went to the privacy page instead and read the partner insights line.

blockers: The trial needs a card number on the first form, and the product has not shown me anything working yet. I stop there.
'Free for 14 days' and 'Web app works today' exist, but there is no way to try it without a card.
friction: The pricing table is wider than a 390 px screen. The two paid plans are cut off and I have to scroll sideways to read the price and the button.
The real price is a footnote: $3.99 is the annual price spread over 12 months, billed as $47.88 at once. Monthly ($5.99) is only in a collapsed FAQ.
The sign-up page says 'Household plan ($47.88/year)' but I never chose Household on that page. It chose for me.
Step indicator says there are three steps, one of them 'Invite your household', but nothing tells me whether I can add Dave before I enter a card.
The hero example is a flatshare. Nothing speaks to a family of four doing a weekly shop.
Product tour is 'coming soon', so I cannot see the scan feature working.
iOS app is 'soon'. I am on an iPhone and the only thing that works today is a web app.

works: Pricing tiers are clear in content: the member cap (5 for Household) matches a family of four.
The sign-up page states in plain words that I will not be charged today and which plan and amount follow.
Expiry nudges plus recipes that use the item up, and the waste report, are real things I do not get from my free list app.
Privacy page is short and readable, and it tells me receipts are kept 30 days.
fails: Card up front for a trial on a product I have not seen work, with the reason given as 'keeps the trial smooth for your whole household'.
Pricing on a phone: half the table is off screen.
'Monthly' price is buried; the headline price is only valid if I pay a year at once.
The partner offers line: 'we may share anonymised and aggregated shopping insights with retail and brand partners', and the sign-up agrees me to partner offers by default in the small print.
No video, no demo, no screenshot of the real app, only a decorative phone mockup.
missing: A way to try it without a card, or a demo of the scan.
Anything about importing a list from another list app, or about my husband joining without a second paid account.
A family example instead of a flatshare.
How cancelling works and where: 'Settings, Billing' is mentioned only for switching to monthly.
Whether the iPhone experience (the web app) works as an installed app, with notifications for expiry.
said: Okay, the price is fine. Four dollars a month is nothing. But why do you want my card before I've seen it do anything?
I tried to look at the pricing on my phone and half the table was off the screen. Does nobody test this on a phone?
My list app is free and Dave already uses it. You'd need to give me something it can't do, and 'expiry nudges' is the only thing I'd even care about.
It's $47.88 a year, not $3.99 a month. Just say that.
'Keeps the trial smooth for your whole household.' That's a non-answer. It's so I forget to cancel.
Show me a video. Anything. 'Coming soon' on a product I'm supposed to pay for?
unsaid: I read the annual-billing footnote and the 'converts to a paid annual plan unless cancelled before day 14' line, and I recognised the pattern straight away. I have been caught by it before with the recipe app and I would put a reminder in my phone for day 12 even if I did sign up. That tells you I do not trust the trial, not that I want it.

The real reason I would not switch is not the product. It is that Dave would have to move, and I do not want to be the one asking him to download another app and re-enter the pantry. Nothing on this site lets me hand him anything or try it with him.

I did not like the partner offers line in the privacy notice. I would not say it out loud, but 'based on your pantry' and a receipt scanner means they know what we buy, and I work in healthcare. I would not put a receipt in there.
I closed the tab at the sign-up form without typing anything. I would not come back to it. If I did, I would have left the pricing page open in a tab for a week as a 'maybe later' and then closed it.
The roommates in the hero made me feel the product was for 25-year-olds. I did not mention it because it is a small thing, but it is why I never got excited.
If the card step had been after a taste of the app, I would probably have gone through. The card wall is the thing that turned 'maybe' into 'not today'.

verdict.why: The idea is solid and the price is fair, but I am happy with a free shared list, switching means persuading my husband, and the trial asks for a card on the first screen before I have seen anything work. On my phone I could not even read the paid plans without swiping sideways.
verdict.what_would_flip: A trial without a card (or a demo/video that shows scan and expiry nudges working), pricing readable on a phone with the monthly price next to the annual one, and a way to bring Dave in without a second paid account.

extra.label: Price I would call fair
extra.value: About $3.99 a month, but only if it is clear that this is what I pay per month and I can pay monthly. Around $30 to $40 a year for the family plan is where I stop thinking about it.

extra.label: Walk-away price
extra.value: Anything over about $6 a month for the Household plan, or $48 a year billed up front without seeing the product work first. The $5.99 monthly price is already too much next to a free app.

extra.label: What I would buy instead
extra.value: Nothing. I would stay on my free shared shopping-list app with Dave and the recipe app I already pay for.

extra.label: What would trigger the purchase
extra.value: Seeing the barcode scan and the expiry nudge work in a real demo, a trial with no card, and a way to bring Dave in so he does not have to be convinced separately. A throwaway pantry from a family of four rather than a flatshare would help.

extra.label: What stops me
extra.value: Card number on the first form, a free competitor I am already happy with, Dave having to switch too, and the privacy notice saying my receipts feed partner insights.
